bibl.title: A Brain System for Auditory Working Memory

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: how a single tone is held in mind for sixteen seconds, and which areas carry the held content
span.quote: The brain basis for auditory working memory, the process of actively maintaining sounds in memory over short periods of time, is controversial. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging in human participants, we demonstrate that the maintenance of single tones in memory is associated with activation in auditory cortex. In addition, sustained activation was observed in hippocampus and inferior frontal gyrus.

span.label: whether auditory cortex is involved in auditory working memory at all, given limited and conflicting evidence
span.quote: In contrast to a number of human neuroimaging studies in the visual domain showing the involvement of early visual areas in working memory ( Pasternak and Greenlee, 2005 ; Postle, 2006 ; for review, see D'Esposito and Postle, 2015 ), evidence for the involvement of auditory cortex in AWM is both limited and conflicting.

span.label: a system in which sound-specific representations in auditory cortex are kept active by long-range connections from hippocampus and frontal cortex
span.quote: The data support a system for auditory working memory based on the maintenance of sound-specific representations in auditory cortex by projections from higher-order areas, including the hippocampus and frontal cortex.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: The data support a system for auditory working memory based on the maintenance of sound-specific representations in auditory cortex by projections from higher-order areas, including the hippocampus and frontal cortex.

span.label: auditory working memory
span.quote: This work concerns the neural bases for human auditory working memory (AWM), the process of keeping sounds in mind for short periods of time when the sounds are no longer present in the environment.

span.label: fmri
span.quote: Using functional magnetic resonance imaging in human participants, we demonstrate that the maintenance of single tones in memory is associated with activation in auditory cortex.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Tone-specific representations in left inferior frontal gyrus drive subvocal rehearsal that re-activates auditory cortex, forming a closed loop that keeps the sound representation alive during the delay
span.quote: Our data, therefore, suggest that HG and LIFG, possibly via PT, form a closed loop where tone-specific representations in the LIFG initiate subvocal rehearsal, which activates the auditory cortex.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Subjects who lose the tone from the focus of attention retrieve it from activated long-term memory, engaging hippocampus but importing proactive interference from tones of previous trials, which is why hippocampal activity tracks poorer accuracy
span.quote: These subjects, however, would perform poorly on the task because recalling the tone from LTM would entail proactive interference from tones that were presented on previous trials, which are also held in LTM; as per the model of Cowan (1995) , these tones are held in the activated part of LTM.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Default-mode-network engagement during the delay indexes mind wandering, which withdraws resources from maintenance and lowers accuracy
span.quote: Greater activation in this network, therefore, implies more mind wandering during the maintenance period and, therefore, poorer performance.

span.label: hippocampal activity here may form part of the activated LTM component of WM, because tones changed across trials and were maintained for long intervals of time (16 s)
span.quote: In our study, we used tones that changed across trials that were maintained for long intervals of time (16 s). It is, therefore, likely that subjects relied on LTM to perform the task activating hippocampus in the process. Activity in hippocampus in that case would form part of the activated LTM component of WM.

span.label: left inferior frontal gyrus and HG may form a closed loop in which tone-specific frontal representations drive subvocal rehearsal that reactivates auditory cortex
span.quote: Our data, therefore, suggest that HG and LIFG, possibly via PT, form a closed loop where tone-specific representations in the LIFG initiate subvocal rehearsal, which activates the auditory cortex.

span.label: a retro-cue protects the cued item from decay, which is why cueing one of two tones gives activation where holding both uncued gave suppression
span.quote: Behavioral studies ( Matsukura et al., 2007 ; Pertzov et al., 2013 ) show that, without any cue, items maintained in memory tend to be forgotten rapidly, but a selective retro-cue leads to protection of the cued item from temporal decay during the maintenance period. It is also known that maintaining multiple items, without a selective cue, leads to diffuse attention ( Makovsik and Jiang, 2007 ) and competition for memory resources, which suppress each other's representation ( Bahcall and Kowler, 1999 ).

span.label: PT may hold symbolic templates further from the sensory pattern, which would make its content harder to decode from blood flow
span.quote: Possible explanations for this finding include the idea that the representation in PT is in the form of high-level symbolic representations or “templates” ( Griffiths and Warren, 2002 ) as opposed to activity in HG that might more closely match the sensory pattern of the stimulus. Templates in PT might be more removed from the stimulus sensory structure and harder to disambiguate based on blood flow patterns.

span.label: posterior hippocampus may be more involved in real-time analysis of auditory stimuli, which predicts stronger connectivity with auditory cortex
span.quote: One possible interpretation is that the posterior hippocampus, compared with the anterior hippocampus, is more involved in the analysis of auditory stimuli in real time, during perception. This in turn predicts greater functional and structural connectivity between auditory cortex and the posterior hippocampus.

span.label: Retrieval-phase activity in the dorsal-anterior right IFG cannot be attributed to retrieval rather than motor response.
span.quote: Regarding daRIFG, which is active only during the retrieval phase, we cannot dissociate whether the activity is related to motor response or to retrieval of WM information.

span.label: The rehearsal interpretation of motor-area activity during maintenance is contested in the wider literature.
span.quote: It should, however, be noted that the role of motor areas in working memory is still controversial as studies using nonrehearsable stimuli also show activity in motor areas during WM ( Liao et al., 2014 ).

span.label: Subjects were not instructed to use any particular strategy, so the subvocal-rehearsal account of the LIFG activity is inferred rather than controlled.
span.quote: Although we did not explicitly instruct the subjects to follow any particular strategy in our study, pitch values of the low tone were in the vocal range that could be rehearsed as a basis for the LIFG activity.

span.label: for the frontal focus active only at retrieval, motor response and memory retrieval cannot be dissociated
span.quote: Regarding daRIFG, which is active only during the retrieval phase, we cannot dissociate whether the activity is related to motor response or to retrieval of WM information.

span.label: no strategy was instructed, so rehearsal is inferred rather than controlled, and the role of motor areas in working memory is itself contested
span.quote: Although we did not explicitly instruct the subjects to follow any particular strategy in our study, pitch values of the low tone were in the vocal range that could be rehearsed as a basis for the LIFG activity. Activation of motor areas during maintenance ( Table 1 ) also support the possibility of rehearsal being used during the maintenance period. It should, however, be noted that the role of motor areas in working memory is still controversial as studies using nonrehearsable stimuli also show activity in motor areas during WM

span.label: classification was above chance in only two of five regions, and in left inferior frontal gyrus five of thirteen subjects fell below chance
span.quote: For HG, 9 of 13 subjects performed above the chance level, 3 performed at chance level, and the performance of 1 subject was below the chance level. For the left IFG, eight subjects were above the chance level and five subjects performed below the chance level.

span.label: three subjects were dropped from the pattern analysis for poor performance but kept in the univariate analysis, because the correlation with behaviour needed them
span.quote: To reduce noise in classification, only trials with correct responses were used. Three subjects who did not perform the task well [they had d -prime (detection) values of 0.89, 0.99, and 1.16, respectively] were dropped from the analysis. We did not drop these subjects from the univariate analysis because we wanted to analyze the correlation of brain activity with behavioral performance.

span.label: multivoxel pattern analysis of the delay period, imported to ask whether auditory delay activity is content-specific
span.quote: Using standard univariate (GLM) analysis, no difference in activity during the maintenance period was found for retention of a low versus a high tone. We used MVPA to test whether patterns of activity during the maintenance period could distinguish between low and high tones.

span.label: the retro-cue, whose protective effect is used to explain why two studies of the same question disagree
span.quote: Behavioral studies ( Matsukura et al., 2007 ; Pertzov et al., 2013 ) show that, without any cue, items maintained in memory tend to be forgotten rapidly, but a selective retro-cue leads to protection of the cued item from temporal decay during the maintenance period. It is also known that maintaining multiple items, without a selective cue, leads to diffuse attention ( Makovsik and Jiang, 2007 ) and competition for memory resources, which suppress each other's representation ( Bahcall and Kowler, 1999 ).

span.label: SUSTAINED ACTIVITY IS NOT WORKING MEMORY: a region can hold information in subthreshold patterns without elevated activity, and elevated activity can reflect sustained attention instead
span.quote: However, a number of recent studies ( Harrison and Tong, 2009 ; Serences et al., 2009 ; Riggall and Postle, 2012 ) have shown that although a brain region may not show elevated activity during the delay period, patterns of subthreshold activity within the same area may nevertheless contain information about the remembered stimulus. Moreover, sustained activity does not imply that the activity is related to WM per se (e.g., it may be related to sustained attention).

span.label: the maintenance regressor is only interpretable because its correlation with the encoding regressor was MEASURED at 0.04 - the phases are adjacent in time and the BOLD response is lagged
span.quote: One concern in WM studies using fMRI is that the maintenance phase immediately follows the encoding phase and, because of the delay intrinsic to the BOLD signal, the regressors for the maintenance and encoding phases may be correlated. The activity observed in the maintenance phase may thus be contaminated with activity during the encoding phase. In our study, because the maintenance duration was much longer than the encoding phase, the correlation coefficient between the encoding and maintenance regressors in the design matrix was very small (0.04). Activity during the maintenance phase is not therefore explained by correlation between the regressors in this design.

span.label: the classifier sees only the middle 10.5 s of the delay, with 4 s trimmed at each end, because the probe tone belonged to the same category and could otherwise leak into the decoding
span.quote: In our experiment, the probe tone presented at the retrieval phase was of the same category that was cued for the maintenance phase. It is, therefore, likely that the probe tone could aid in the classification of tones during the maintenance phase (because of the common variance captured by maintenance and recall phase regressors). To ensure that this was not so, only the middle 10.5 s of the maintenance period was modeled, leaving 4 s on either side based on recommendations by Zarahn et al. (1997) .

span.label: connectivity is never compared with rest, because heart rate and other physiological variables differ between task and rest and are known to confound functional connectivity
span.quote: We compared the encoding, maintenance, and retrieval conditions against each other instead of comparing each of these against baseline. This is because physiological variables such as heart rate during cognitive tasks (here, working memory) are different from the rest condition ( Middleton et al., 1999 ), and changes in physiological variables are known to confound functional connectivity in fMRI ( Birn, 2012 ). Since the physiological parameters will be similar across encoding, maintenance, and retrieval conditions compared with any of these conditions against baseline, to minimize the effect of physiological noise on the connectivity analysis, we report the comparison in connectivity among the three conditions.

span.label: the inclusion criteria differ BY ANALYSIS and each difference is justified: poor performers are excluded from classification to reduce noise and retained in the univariate analysis because the brain-behaviour correlation requires the spread
span.quote: To reduce noise in classification, only trials with correct responses were used. Three subjects who did not perform the task well [they had d -prime (detection) values of 0.89, 0.99, and 1.16, respectively] were dropped from the analysis. We did not drop these subjects from the univariate analysis because we wanted to analyze the correlation of brain activity with behavioral performance.

span.label: d-PRIME is d', the signal-detection sensitivity index, and not a priming prime despite carrying the word: it is the per-subject detection measure (0.89, 0.99, 1.16) used as the exclusion criterion for the pattern analysis
span.quote: To reduce noise in classification, only trials with correct responses were used. Three subjects who did not perform the task well [they had d -prime (detection) values of 0.89, 0.99, and 1.16, respectively] were dropped from the analysis. We did not drop these subjects from the univariate analysis because we wanted to analyze the correlation of brain activity with behavioral performance.

span.label: contradicts → Linke et al. (2011)
span.quote: We observed sustained activation of the auditory cortex during a maintenance period, which is in contrast to findings from Linke et al. (2011) , who observed suppression during maintenance.

span.label: replicates → Linke and Cusack (2015)
span.quote: The later study of Linke and Cusack (2015) , which required maintenance of a single sound in WM showed activation during maintenance, like the present study.

span.label: builds-on → Jeneson and Squire (2011)
span.quote: In light of the proposal by Jeneson and Squire (2011) , we predicted that subjects who could not maintain a sustained focus of attention on the tone to be maintained would rely more on LTM, and, therefore, hippocampus would be activated to a greater extent in these subjects.

span.label: contradicts → Linke 2011's observation of suppression in auditory cortex during maintenance of two tones
span.quote: We observed sustained activation of the auditory cortex during a maintenance period, which is in contrast to findings from Linke et al. (2011) , who observed suppression during maintenance. This might be attributable to differences in the task in the two studies. While Linke et al. (2011) required subjects to maintain two tones from different categories without any cue before or after the tones, participants in the present study were explicitly instructed to maintain one of the two tones after the tones were presented (retro-cue).

span.label: reconciles → the conflicting reports of increased and decreased auditory cortical activity during auditory working memory
span.quote: Behavioral studies ( Matsukura et al., 2007 ; Pertzov et al., 2013 ) show that, without any cue, items maintained in memory tend to be forgotten rapidly, but a selective retro-cue leads to protection of the cued item from temporal decay during the maintenance period. It is also known that maintaining multiple items, without a selective cue, leads to diffuse attention ( Makovsik and Jiang, 2007 ) and competition for memory resources, which suppress each other's representation ( Bahcall and Kowler, 1999 ).

span.label: confirms → Linke and Cusack 2015's activation during maintenance of a single sound
span.quote: The later study of Linke and Cusack (2015) , which required maintenance of a single sound in WM showed activation during maintenance, like the present study.

span.label: supports → Jeneson and Squire's account in which hippocampal activity during working memory reflects recourse to long-term memory
span.quote: In light of the proposal by Jeneson and Squire (2011) , we predicted that subjects who could not maintain a sustained focus of attention on the tone to be maintained would rely more on LTM, and, therefore, hippocampus would be activated to a greater extent in these subjects. These subjects, however, would perform poorly on the task because recalling the tone from LTM would entail proactive interference from tones that were presented on previous trials, which are also held in LTM; as per the model of Cowan (1995) , these tones are held in the activated part of LTM. A negative correlation between hippocampus activity and behavioral performance is thus expected.

span.label: builds-on → visual working memory studies showing content-specific subthreshold activity during the delay
span.quote: However, a number of recent studies ( Harrison and Tong, 2009 ; Serences et al., 2009 ; Riggall and Postle, 2012 ) have shown that although a brain region may not show elevated activity during the delay period, patterns of subthreshold activity within the same area may nevertheless contain information about the remembered stimulus. Moreover, sustained activity does not imply that the activity is related to WM per se (e.g., it may be related to sustained attention).

span.label: sustained activity —distinct-from→ WM
span.quote: However, a number of recent studies ( Harrison and Tong, 2009 ; Serences et al., 2009 ; Riggall and Postle, 2012 ) have shown that although a brain region may not show elevated activity during the delay period, patterns of subthreshold activity within the same area may nevertheless contain information about the remembered stimulus. Moreover, sustained activity does not imply that the activity is related to WM per se (e.g., it may be related to sustained attention).

span.label: MVPA —operationalised-as→ maintenance
span.quote: Using standard univariate (GLM) analysis, no difference in activity during the maintenance period was found for retention of a low versus a high tone. We used MVPA to test whether patterns of activity during the maintenance period could distinguish between low and high tones.

span.label: encoding —distinct-from→ maintenance
span.quote: One concern in WM studies using fMRI is that the maintenance phase immediately follows the encoding phase and, because of the delay intrinsic to the BOLD signal, the regressors for the maintenance and encoding phases may be correlated. The activity observed in the maintenance phase may thus be contaminated with activity during the encoding phase. In our study, because the maintenance duration was much longer than the encoding phase, the correlation coefficient between the encoding and maintenance regressors in the design matrix was very small (0.04). Activity during the maintenance phase is not therefore explained by correlation between the regressors in this design.

span.label: retrieval —distinct-from→ maintenance
span.quote: In our experiment, the probe tone presented at the retrieval phase was of the same category that was cued for the maintenance phase. It is, therefore, likely that the probe tone could aid in the classification of tones during the maintenance phase (because of the common variance captured by maintenance and recall phase regressors). To ensure that this was not so, only the middle 10.5 s of the maintenance period was modeled, leaving 4 s on either side based on recommendations by Zarahn et al. (1997) .

span.label: HG —contrasted-with→ PT
span.quote: During maintenance ( Fig. 2 A , middle row), significant activity in the auditory cortex was mostly confined to PT bilaterally: of all the voxels that survived threshold, 84.42% were located in the PT. The percentages in the medial, middle, and lateral part of HG were 3.19%, 5.59%, and 6.79%, respectively.

span.label: LIFG —contrasted-with→ RIFG
span.quote: Is the sustained activity in LIFG and RIFG specific to the information held in WM? Application of MVPA to these ROIs showed that, while patterns of activity in the LIFG could distinguish which of the two tones was held in WM, the RIFG could not.

span.label: hippocampus —operationalised-as→ LTM
span.quote: In our study, we used tones that changed across trials that were maintained for long intervals of time (16 s). It is, therefore, likely that subjects relied on LTM to perform the task activating hippocampus in the process. Activity in hippocampus in that case would form part of the activated LTM component of WM.

span.label: RETRACTED (TWO EFFECTS OF A COMMON CAUSE, TAGGED AS CAUSING EACH OTHER - a class I have not named before) · hippocampus —causes→ behavioral performance
span.quote: In light of the proposal by Jeneson and Squire (2011) , we predicted that subjects who could not maintain a sustained focus of attention on the tone to be maintained would rely more on LTM, and, therefore, hippocampus would be activated to a greater extent in these subjects. These subjects, however, would perform poorly on the task because recalling the tone from LTM would entail proactive interference from tones that were presented on previous trials, which are also held in LTM; as per the model of Cowan (1995) , these tones are held in the activated part of LTM. A negative correlation between hippocampus activity and behavioral performance is thus expected.

span.label: DMN —causes→ behavioral performance
span.quote: Negative correlation between activity in a set of areas that together comprise the DMN, and behavioral performance was observed. The DMN is known to be active in mind wandering ( Mason et al., 2007 ). Greater activation in this network, therefore, implies more mind wandering during the maintenance period and, therefore, poorer performance.

span.label: IFJ —causes→ LTM
span.quote: Negative correlation was also observed in the right IFJ. Evidence ( Roth and Courtney, 2007 ) shows that IFJ is involved in updating the contents of WM from LTM. The subjects who used LTM to perform the task activated the IFJ more but (as explained above in the case for hippocampus) performed poorly, which explains the negative correlation observed in IFJ.

span.label: retro-cue —causes→ auditory cortex
span.quote: We observed sustained activation of the auditory cortex during a maintenance period, which is in contrast to findings from Linke et al. (2011) , who observed suppression during maintenance. This might be attributable to differences in the task in the two studies. While Linke et al. (2011) required subjects to maintain two tones from different categories without any cue before or after the tones, participants in the present study were explicitly instructed to maintain one of the two tones after the tones were presented (retro-cue).

span.label: rehearsal —operationalised-as→ LIFG
span.quote: Although we did not explicitly instruct the subjects to follow any particular strategy in our study, pitch values of the low tone were in the vocal range that could be rehearsed as a basis for the LIFG activity. Activation of motor areas during maintenance ( Table 1 ) also support the possibility of rehearsal being used during the maintenance period. It should, however, be noted that the role of motor areas in working memory is still controversial as studies using nonrehearsable stimuli also show activity in motor areas during WM

span.label: PPI —operationalised-as→ connectivity
span.quote: Connectivity analysis was conducted using psychophysiological interactions (PPIs) as implemented in the CONN toolbox

span.label: auditory cortex —causes→ hippocampus
span.quote: Connectivity during maintenance compared with encoding (2) Auditory cortex is strongly connected to the right hippocampus (right HG and right PT are connected to the right posterior hippocampus, and left PT is connected to the right anterior hippocampus). (3) Auditory cortex is strongly connected to left IFG; both left HG and PT in each hemisphere are connected to left IFG.

span.label: auditory cortex —causes→ LIFG
span.quote: Connectivity of LIFG with the auditory cortex during the maintenance period is consistent with the role of LIFG in keeping the representations active in auditory cortex by subvocal rehearsal of the tones.

span.label: t-test
span.quote: Given that we were interested in whether results were significantly above chance, one-tailed t tests were used for testing the statistical significance of classification.

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: A two-way repeated-measures ANOVA for maintenance data with hemisphere (left and right) and ROI (medial HG, middle HG, lateral HG and PT) as factors showed a main effect of ROI ( F (3,45) = 15.70, p < 0.001), no main effect of hemisphere ( F (1,15) = 3.96, p = 0.065), and no interaction ( F (3,45) = 1.16, p = 0.33).

span.label: general linear model
span.quote: After preprocessing, a general linear model (GLM) was used for statistical analysis.

span.label: regression
span.quote: The correlation of brain activity with behavioral performance at group level was performed using regression analysis with age of the subjects as a regressor of no interest.

span.label: multiple-comparison correction (false discovery rate)
span.quote: The group-level connectivity between the regions was corrected for multiple comparisons using the false discovery rate method.

span.label: permutation test
span.quote: To make sure that the statistical significance of our MVPA results was not biased by the assumptions of the parametric t test, we also evaluated the statistical significance using a nonparametric test for MVPA as proposed in the study by Stelzer et al. (2013) .

span.label: cross-validation
span.quote: The SVM classifier, as implemented in the LIBSVM toolbox ( Chang and Lin, 2011 ), was used with the following leave-one-session-out cross-validation strategy: the classifier was trained on data from three of the four sessions and tested on the left-out session.

span.label: small-volume correction
span.quote: Given prior hypotheses about the involvement of auditory cortex and hippocampus in WM, small-volume correction (using anatomically defined volumes) was used for auditory cortex and hippocampus.

span.label: psychophysiological interaction analysis
span.quote: Connectivity analysis was conducted using psychophysiological interactions (PPIs) as implemented in the CONN toolbox ( Whitfield-Gabrieli and Nieto-Castanon, 2012 ).

span.label: support vector machine
span.quote: Using standard univariate (GLM) analysis, no difference in activity during the maintenance period was found for retention of a low versus a high tone. We used MVPA to test whether patterns of activity during the maintenance period could distinguish between low and high tones.

span.label: false discovery rate
span.quote: We compared the encoding, maintenance, and retrieval conditions against each other instead of comparing each of these against baseline. This is because physiological variables such as heart rate during cognitive tasks (here, working memory) are different from the rest condition ( Middleton et al., 1999 ), and changes in physiological variables are known to confound functional connectivity in fMRI ( Birn, 2012 ). Since the physiological parameters will be similar across encoding, maintenance, and retrieval conditions compared with any of these conditions against baseline, to minimize the effect of physiological noise on the connectivity analysis, we report the comparison in connectivity among the three conditions.

span.label: one-tailed t tests
span.quote: To make sure that the statistical significance of our MVPA results was not biased by the assumptions of the parametric t test, we also evaluated the statistical significance using a nonparametric test for MVPA as proposed in the study by Stelzer et al. (2013) . Briefly, we first randomized the target labels and ran the MVPA for each subject 200 times. For each subject, then, one accuracy value (of the 200 above) was picked up randomly and averaged across subjects. This procedure was repeated 100,000 times to obtain 100,000 accuracy values, which represent the null distribution for group accuracy. The p value for the group accuracy with correct labels is then determined based on this null distribution. Using this procedure the p values obtained for HG and left IFG are 0.0013 and 0.015, respectively. These values are almost identical to the p values using the t test.

span.label: During the 16 s maintenance period, sustained auditory-cortex activity was concentrated in PT, with 84.42% of suprathreshold voxels lying there.
span.quote: During maintenance ( Fig. 2 A , middle row), significant activity in the auditory cortex was mostly confined to PT bilaterally: of all the voxels that survived threshold, 84.42% were located in the PT.

span.label: Contrary to earlier reports of suppression, auditory cortex showed no activity suppression in any phase of the working-memory task.
span.quote: No suppression of activity was observed in auditory cortex during any of the three phases of the task.

span.label: Only HG (55.61%) and left inferior frontal gyrus (54.25%) carried information about whether a low or high tone was being held; PT, hippocampus and right inferior frontal gyrus classified at chance.
span.quote: Only two regions, HG and left IFG, showed an above-chance level classification at the p < 0.05 level (HG: accuracy = 55.61%, t (12) = 3.82, p = 0.001; PT: accuracy = 49.08%, t (12) = −0.51, p = 0.69; hippocampus: accuracy = 49.26%, t (12) = −0.38, p = 0.64; left IFG: accuracy = 54.25%, t (12) = 2.41, p = 0.016; right IFG: accuracy = 48.87%, t (12) = −0.51, p = 0.69).

span.label: Univariate analysis found no mean-activity difference between holding a low versus a high tone, so tone identity was recoverable only from multivoxel patterns.
span.quote: Using standard univariate (GLM) analysis, no difference in activity during the maintenance period was found for retention of a low versus a high tone.

span.label: Hippocampus was significantly active in all three phases of the task - encoding, maintenance and retrieval.
span.quote: Significant activity was observed during encoding (peak at MNI coordinates 18, −30, −6; t (15) = 11.65), maintenance (peak at MNI coordinates −10, −34, −8; t (15) = 7.62), and retrieval (peak at MNI coordinates −18, −26, −10; t (15) = 10.85).

span.label: Along the hippocampal long axis, encoding activity was stronger anteriorly and retrieval activity stronger posteriorly.
span.quote: On comparing the activity during encoding and retrieval, we observed greater activity for encoding in the anterior hippocampus (encoding > retrieval; peak at MNI coordinates 26, −10, −16; t (15) = 3.23) and greater activity for retrieval in the posterior hippocampus (retrieval > encoding; peak at −16, −26, −12; t (15) = 7.51).

span.label: Hippocampal activity during maintenance correlated negatively with task accuracy: subjects with more hippocampal activity performed worse.
span.quote: This is exactly what we observed: activity in both left and right hippocampi increased with poorer performance.

span.label: Relative to encoding, maintenance was accompanied by long-range functional connectivity from auditory cortex to the right anterior and posterior hippocampus.
span.quote: (2) Auditory cortex is strongly connected to the right hippocampus (right HG and right PT are connected to the right posterior hippocampus, and left PT is connected to the right anterior hippocampus).

span.label: no suppression of auditory cortical activity was seen in any phase of the task
span.quote: No suppression of activity was observed in auditory cortex during any of the three phases of the task.

span.label: during maintenance 84.42 percent of surviving auditory voxels lay in PT
span.quote: During maintenance ( Fig. 2 A , middle row), significant activity in the auditory cortex was mostly confined to PT bilaterally: of all the voxels that survived threshold, 84.42% were located in the PT. The percentages in the medial, middle, and lateral part of HG were 3.19%, 5.59%, and 6.79%, respectively.

span.label: hippocampal activity was constant along the anterior-posterior axis during maintenance but rose posteriorly during encoding and retrieval
span.quote: There was a gradual increase in activity from approximately the middle of the axis ( y = −20) to the posterior end of the axis during retrieval in both hippocampi. A similar increase (more in the right than in the left hippocampus) was also observed during the encoding phase. During the maintenance phase, however, activity was almost constant throughout the anterior–posterior axis.

span.label: THE UNIVARIATE NULL THAT MOTIVATED THE PATTERN ANALYSIS: mean activity did not differ between holding a low and a high tone
span.quote: Using standard univariate (GLM) analysis, no difference in activity during the maintenance period was found for retention of a low versus a high tone. We used MVPA to test whether patterns of activity during the maintenance period could distinguish between low and high tones.

span.label: only HG at 55.61 percent and left inferior frontal gyrus at 54.25 percent classified the held tone above chance
span.quote: Only two regions, HG and left IFG, showed an above-chance level classification at the p < 0.05 level (HG: accuracy = 55.61%, t (12) = 3.82, p = 0.001; PT: accuracy = 49.08%, t (12) = −0.51, p = 0.69; hippocampus: accuracy = 49.26%, t (12) = −0.38, p = 0.64; left IFG: accuracy = 54.25%, t (12) = 2.41, p = 0.016; right IFG: accuracy = 48.87%, t (12) = −0.51, p = 0.69).

span.label: AND THE PER-SUBJECT SPLIT IS REPORTED: 9 of 13 above chance in HG, and only 8 of 13 in left inferior frontal gyrus
span.quote: For HG, 9 of 13 subjects performed above the chance level, 3 performed at chance level, and the performance of 1 subject was below the chance level. For the left IFG, eight subjects were above the chance level and five subjects performed below the chance level.

span.label: PARAMETRIC ASSUMPTION CHECKED: a permutation test over 100,000 resamples gave p values almost identical to the t tests
span.quote: To make sure that the statistical significance of our MVPA results was not biased by the assumptions of the parametric t test, we also evaluated the statistical significance using a nonparametric test for MVPA as proposed in the study by Stelzer et al. (2013) . Briefly, we first randomized the target labels and ran the MVPA for each subject 200 times. For each subject, then, one accuracy value (of the 200 above) was picked up randomly and averaged across subjects. This procedure was repeated 100,000 times to obtain 100,000 accuracy values, which represent the null distribution for group accuracy. The p value for the group accuracy with correct labels is then determined based on this null distribution. Using this procedure the p values obtained for HG and left IFG are 0.0013 and 0.015, respectively. These values are almost identical to the p values using the t test.

span.label: THE REGRESSOR CONFOUND MEASURED: encoding and maintenance regressors correlated at only 0.04
span.quote: One concern in WM studies using fMRI is that the maintenance phase immediately follows the encoding phase and, because of the delay intrinsic to the BOLD signal, the regressors for the maintenance and encoding phases may be correlated. The activity observed in the maintenance phase may thus be contaminated with activity during the encoding phase. In our study, because the maintenance duration was much longer than the encoding phase, the correlation coefficient between the encoding and maintenance regressors in the design matrix was very small (0.04). Activity during the maintenance phase is not therefore explained by correlation between the regressors in this design.

span.label: and the analysis was repeated on only the middle of the delay period, with very similar results
span.quote: We also repeated the univariate analysis by leaving 4 s on either side of the maintenance phase [i.e., modeling only the middle portion (10.5 s) of the maintenance phase; Zarahn et al., 1997 ] to avoid any possibility of “lagged” blood flow changes during maintenance affecting the maintenance measurements. The results of this analysis were very similar to the one using all of the maintenance period.

span.label: DECODING LEAKAGE PREVENTED: the probe belonged to the cued category, so 4 s was trimmed from each end before classification
span.quote: In our experiment, the probe tone presented at the retrieval phase was of the same category that was cued for the maintenance phase. It is, therefore, likely that the probe tone could aid in the classification of tones during the maintenance phase (because of the common variance captured by maintenance and recall phase regressors). To ensure that this was not so, only the middle 10.5 s of the maintenance period was modeled, leaving 4 s on either side based on recommendations by Zarahn et al. (1997) .

span.label: THE REST BASELINE WAS REFUSED for connectivity, because physiological variables differ between task and rest and confound functional connectivity
span.quote: We compared the encoding, maintenance, and retrieval conditions against each other instead of comparing each of these against baseline. This is because physiological variables such as heart rate during cognitive tasks (here, working memory) are different from the rest condition ( Middleton et al., 1999 ), and changes in physiological variables are known to confound functional connectivity in fMRI ( Birn, 2012 ). Since the physiological parameters will be similar across encoding, maintenance, and retrieval conditions compared with any of these conditions against baseline, to minimize the effect of physiological noise on the connectivity analysis, we report the comparison in connectivity among the three conditions.

span.label: INCLUSION CRITERIA DIFFER BY ANALYSIS, each justified: three poor performers dropped from classification and kept in the univariate analysis
span.quote: To reduce noise in classification, only trials with correct responses were used. Three subjects who did not perform the task well [they had d -prime (detection) values of 0.89, 0.99, and 1.16, respectively] were dropped from the analysis. We did not drop these subjects from the univariate analysis because we wanted to analyze the correlation of brain activity with behavioral performance.

span.label: A PREDICTION DERIVED FROM THE RIVAL'S MODEL: if hippocampal activity means falling back on long-term memory, it should correlate NEGATIVELY with performance
span.quote: In light of the proposal by Jeneson and Squire (2011) , we predicted that subjects who could not maintain a sustained focus of attention on the tone to be maintained would rely more on LTM, and, therefore, hippocampus would be activated to a greater extent in these subjects. These subjects, however, would perform poorly on the task because recalling the tone from LTM would entail proactive interference from tones that were presented on previous trials, which are also held in LTM; as per the model of Cowan (1995) , these tones are held in the activated part of LTM. A negative correlation between hippocampus activity and behavioral performance is thus expected.

span.label: and that is what was found - activity in both hippocampi increased as performance worsened
span.quote: This is exactly what we observed: activity in both left and right hippocampi increased with poorer performance. Furthermore, we also observed a negative correlation with behavior during recall in retrosplenial cortex, which has been known to be involved in retrieval of long-term memories ( Vann et al., 2009 ; Rugg and Vilberg, 2013 ; Kumar et al., 2014a ). This is also consistent with retrieval of LTM during task performance.

span.label: default mode network activity also correlated negatively with performance, read as mind wandering
span.quote: Negative correlation between activity in a set of areas that together comprise the DMN, and behavioral performance was observed. The DMN is known to be active in mind wandering ( Mason et al., 2007 ). Greater activation in this network, therefore, implies more mind wandering during the maintenance period and, therefore, poorer performance.

span.label: as did right inferior frontal junction activity, read as updating working memory from long-term memory
span.quote: Negative correlation was also observed in the right IFJ. Evidence ( Roth and Courtney, 2007 ) shows that IFJ is involved in updating the contents of WM from LTM. The subjects who used LTM to perform the task activated the IFJ more but (as explained above in the case for hippocampus) performed poorly, which explains the negative correlation observed in IFJ.

span.label: parietal activity correlated POSITIVELY with performance, read as sustained attention
span.quote: During the maintenance period, we observed a positive correlation with activity in part of parietal cortex which has been shown to be involved in maintaining sustained attention ( Foucher et al., 2004 ). Subjects who could keep sustained attention during the maintenance period performed better on the task.

span.label: A CONTRADICTION RESOLVED BY A DESIGN VARIABLE: the earlier suppression finding used two uncued tones, this study cued one of two after presentation
span.quote: We observed sustained activation of the auditory cortex during a maintenance period, which is in contrast to findings from Linke et al. (2011) , who observed suppression during maintenance. This might be attributable to differences in the task in the two studies. While Linke et al. (2011) required subjects to maintain two tones from different categories without any cue before or after the tones, participants in the present study were explicitly instructed to maintain one of the two tones after the tones were presented (retro-cue).

span.label: and a later study holding a single sound found activation, agreeing with this one
span.quote: The later study of Linke and Cusack (2015) , which required maintenance of a single sound in WM showed activation during maintenance, like the present study.

span.label: long-range connectivity of auditory cortex was ABSENT during encoding, appearing only during maintenance
span.quote: There is no long-range connectivity of the auditory cortex; both HG and PT in each hemisphere are connected to each other, but there is no connectivity of these regions outside the auditory cortex

span.label: during maintenance auditory cortex connected to right hippocampus and to left inferior frontal gyrus
span.quote: Connectivity during maintenance compared with encoding (2) Auditory cortex is strongly connected to the right hippocampus (right HG and right PT are connected to the right posterior hippocampus, and left PT is connected to the right anterior hippocampus). (3) Auditory cortex is strongly connected to left IFG; both left HG and PT in each hemisphere are connected to left IFG.

span.label: accuracy ranged from 67 to 98 percent and was better for the first tone than the second
span.quote: The overall accuracy scores of participants varied from 67% to 98% (mean, 83.5%; SD, 10%). Accuracy was better when cued to retain the first tone compared with the second tone (first tone, 85.7%; second tone, 81.3%; t (15) = 2.68, p < 0.017).

span.label: seventeen adults with normal hearing and no musical training took part
span.quote: Seventeen healthy adults (8 females; mean age, 29.5 years; age range, 19–52 years) participated in this study after providing written informed consent to undergo procedures approved by the local ethics committee. Participants were paid for their participation and were selected based on the following criteria: normal hearing and no musical training.

span.label: auditory working memory (AWM)
span.quote: This work concerns the neural bases for human auditory working memory (AWM), the process of keeping sounds in mind for short periods of time when the sounds are no longer present in the environment.

span.label: multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA)
span.quote: The principal aim of MVPA is to determine whether patterns of activity in a given area can distinguish between two or more experimental conditions ( Haynes and Rees, 2006 ; Norman et al., 2006 ).

span.label: activated LTM component of working memory
span.term: activated LTM component of working memory
span.quote: The latter component constitutes an “activated LTM” component of WM ( Cowan, 1995 ).

span.label: AWM
span.quote: The brain basis for auditory working memory, the process of actively maintaining sounds in memory over short periods of time, is controversial. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging in human participants, we demonstrate that the maintenance of single tones in memory is associated with activation in auditory cortex. In addition, sustained activation was observed in hippocampus and inferior frontal gyrus.

span.label: MVPA
span.quote: Using standard univariate (GLM) analysis, no difference in activity during the maintenance period was found for retention of a low versus a high tone. We used MVPA to test whether patterns of activity during the maintenance period could distinguish between low and high tones.

span.label: activated LTM
span.quote: In our study, we used tones that changed across trials that were maintained for long intervals of time (16 s). It is, therefore, likely that subjects relied on LTM to perform the task activating hippocampus in the process. Activity in hippocampus in that case would form part of the activated LTM component of WM.

span.label: which of the two tones (low or high) was cued for maintenance
span.term: which of the two tones (low or high) was cued for maintenance
span.quote: Whether tone 1 or tone 2 had to be held in mind was randomized.

span.label: task phase (encoding, maintenance, retrieval)
span.quote: The following events were included in the design matrix and modeled as three regressors: (1) an encoding period modeled as a single block of 3 s (1 s alert plus 2 s sound); (2) a maintenance period with onset starting from the onset of cue and of duration 18.5 s (2.5 s Cue period plus 16 s); and (3) a retrieval period modeled as a block of 3 s after the maintenance period.

span.label: BOLD activity in each region of interest
span.term: BOLD activity in each region of interest
span.quote: To further confirm the activation of auditory cortex during the maintenance phase, we extracted BOLD time series from each of the ROIs (for details, see Materials and Methods).

span.label: behavioural accuracy on the same/different probe decision
span.term: behavioural accuracy on the same/different probe decision
span.quote: The overall accuracy scores of participants varied from 67% to 98% (mean, 83.5%; SD, 10%).

span.label: subject age
span.quote: The correlation of brain activity with behavioral performance at group level was performed using regression analysis with age of the subjects as a regressor of no interest.

span.label: head motion and physiological noise
span.quote: The design matrix also included physiological and motion regressors of no interest.

span.label: participant hearing status and musical training
span.term: participant hearing status and musical training
span.quote: Participants were paid for their participation and were selected based on the following criteria: normal hearing and no musical training.

span.label: maintenance
span.quote: One concern in WM studies using fMRI is that the maintenance phase immediately follows the encoding phase and, because of the delay intrinsic to the BOLD signal, the regressors for the maintenance and encoding phases may be correlated. The activity observed in the maintenance phase may thus be contaminated with activity during the encoding phase. In our study, because the maintenance duration was much longer than the encoding phase, the correlation coefficient between the encoding and maintenance regressors in the design matrix was very small (0.04). Activity during the maintenance phase is not therefore explained by correlation between the regressors in this design.

span.label: sustained activity
span.quote: However, a number of recent studies ( Harrison and Tong, 2009 ; Serences et al., 2009 ; Riggall and Postle, 2012 ) have shown that although a brain region may not show elevated activity during the delay period, patterns of subthreshold activity within the same area may nevertheless contain information about the remembered stimulus. Moreover, sustained activity does not imply that the activity is related to WM per se (e.g., it may be related to sustained attention).

span.label: 16 s — duration for which a single cued tone had to be held in working memory
span.quote: To address these questions, we measured the fMRI BOLD response while subjects, after listening to a pair of tones, were then cued to maintain either a low or a high tone for 16 s.

span.label: Seventeen healthy adults — number of participants recruited for the fMRI experiment
span.quote: Seventeen healthy adults (8 females; mean age, 29.5 years; age range, 19–52 years) participated in this study after providing written informed consent to undergo procedures approved by the local ethics committee.

span.label: 67% to 98% (mean, 83.5%; SD, 10%) — range and mean of participants' overall task accuracy
span.quote: The overall accuracy scores of participants varied from 67% to 98% (mean, 83.5%; SD, 10%).

span.label: first tone, 85.7%; second tone, 81.3% — accuracy advantage for retaining the first rather than the second tone of the pair
span.quote: Accuracy was better when cued to retain the first tone compared with the second tone (first tone, 85.7%; second tone, 81.3%; t (15) = 2.68, p < 0.017).

span.label: 0.04 — correlation between the encoding and maintenance regressors in the design matrix, used to argue maintenance activity is not contaminated by encoding
span.quote: In our study, because the maintenance duration was much longer than the encoding phase, the correlation coefficient between the encoding and maintenance regressors in the design matrix was very small (0.04).

span.label: 100,000 — number of resamples used to build the null distribution for group classification accuracy
span.quote: This procedure was repeated 100,000 times to obtain 100,000 accuracy values, which represent the null distribution for group accuracy.

span.label: 0.0013 and 0.015 — nonparametric p values for above-chance decoding in HG and left inferior frontal gyrus, matching the parametric t test values
span.quote: Using this procedure the p values obtained for HG and left IFG are 0.0013 and 0.015, respectively.

span.label: 0.04 — correlation between encoding and maintenance regressors, the measured bound on contamination
span.quote: One concern in WM studies using fMRI is that the maintenance phase immediately follows the encoding phase and, because of the delay intrinsic to the BOLD signal, the regressors for the maintenance and encoding phases may be correlated. The activity observed in the maintenance phase may thus be contaminated with activity during the encoding phase. In our study, because the maintenance duration was much longer than the encoding phase, the correlation coefficient between the encoding and maintenance regressors in the design matrix was very small (0.04). Activity during the maintenance phase is not therefore explained by correlation between the regressors in this design.

span.label: 55.61% and 54.25% — above-chance classification accuracy in HG and left IFG, where chance is 50%
span.quote: Only two regions, HG and left IFG, showed an above-chance level classification at the p < 0.05 level (HG: accuracy = 55.61%, t (12) = 3.82, p = 0.001; PT: accuracy = 49.08%, t (12) = −0.51, p = 0.69; hippocampus: accuracy = 49.26%, t (12) = −0.38, p = 0.64; left IFG: accuracy = 54.25%, t (12) = 2.41, p = 0.016; right IFG: accuracy = 48.87%, t (12) = −0.51, p = 0.69).

span.label: 9 of 13 and 8 of 13 — subjects above chance in the two decodable regions
span.quote: For HG, 9 of 13 subjects performed above the chance level, 3 performed at chance level, and the performance of 1 subject was below the chance level. For the left IFG, eight subjects were above the chance level and five subjects performed below the chance level.

span.label: 84.42% — share of maintenance-surviving auditory voxels lying in PT
span.quote: During maintenance ( Fig. 2 A , middle row), significant activity in the auditory cortex was mostly confined to PT bilaterally: of all the voxels that survived threshold, 84.42% were located in the PT. The percentages in the medial, middle, and lateral part of HG were 3.19%, 5.59%, and 6.79%, respectively.

span.label: 67% to 98% — range of behavioural accuracy across subjects, the spread the correlations depend on
span.quote: The overall accuracy scores of participants varied from 67% to 98% (mean, 83.5%; SD, 10%). Accuracy was better when cued to retain the first tone compared with the second tone (first tone, 85.7%; second tone, 81.3%; t (15) = 2.68, p < 0.017).
